Before your interview, develop one practical skill: draw the payment chain from airline to engine manufacturer to repair provider and supplier, then explain it aloud without notes. Label what triggers each payment and who bears an unexpected covered repair bill. Use the TotalCare description and the annual report to check your explanation; do not invent a price per hour where commercial terms are undisclosed. Tomorrow, supplier bargaining power explains why collecting the airline’s payment does not give the manufacturer complete control over the repair costs underneath it.

title: Power Follows the Cost of Switching
takeaway: A company gains bargaining power when its customer cannot replace it without costly delays, technical work, or approvals.
slide_title: Recap: Put Your Role on the Map
body: Yesterday, you worked with the industry's basic map: manufacturers deliver aircraft and spacecraft, suppliers provide the systems and parts, and maintenance, repair, and overhaul businesses keep equipment in service. Keep that same map today. Whether you join engineering, purchasing, finance, or maintenance, your work sits between organizations that buy, build, accept, or repair something. Start by locating your employer and its immediate customer; those are the familiar actors we will use to examine power.

title: Power Follows the Cost of Switching
takeaway: A company gains bargaining power when its customer cannot replace it without costly delays, technical work, or approvals.
body: Switching costs are the money, time, and technical work needed to replace a supplier with an acceptable alternative. Those costs create bargaining power: the harder the replacement, the harder it is for a customer to reject the supplier's terms. An original equipment manufacturer may award the contract, yet still depend heavily on a smaller supplier's tooling, production knowledge, and accepted processes. This applies down the supplier tiers and into maintenance. Acceptance may come from the manufacturer, a military or space customer, or a regulator; it is not always a new government certification. In your daily work, ask more than who owns the purchase order. Ask what would have to happen before another source could deliver something the customer would accept.

title: Power Follows the Cost of Switching
takeaway: A company gains bargaining power when its customer cannot replace it without costly delays, technical work, or approvals.
body: Consider a buyer supporting Boeing's 737, for which Spirit AeroSystems supplies fuselages. Boeing pays Spirit for contracted work; Spirit pays its own suppliers. Boeing controls its purchasing decision, but another company cannot immediately supply an interchangeable, accepted fuselage. Replacement would require access to the design, tooling, trained workers, production capacity, and evidence that the output meets requirements. Boeing's technical and quality teams would assess the new source, with regulatory involvement where required. Until that work is complete, deliveries still depend on the existing source. That gives Spirit leverage, while Spirit's dependence on Boeing's orders gives Boeing leverage in return. For your role, the practical task is to document the replacement path and its longest delay, not simply collect a cheaper quotation.

title: Power Follows the Cost of Switching
takeaway: A company gains bargaining power when its customer cannot replace it without costly delays, technical work, or approvals.
body: On July 1, 2024, Boeing announced a definitive agreement to acquire Spirit AeroSystems in an all-stock transaction valued at approximately $4.7 billion in equity, or approximately $8.3 billion including Spirit's last reported net debt. Boeing said reintegration would align production systems, safety, and quality. The outcome at that announcement was an acquisition agreement, not a completed takeover or proof of improved performance. It illustrates a response to deep supplier dependence: seek ownership rather than assume a replacement can be bought off the shelf. Switching costs help explain that choice, but were not Boeing's only stated concern. An interview question is, 'Why not just change suppliers?' Structure your answer around the existing dependency, the replacement work, and the decision to bring that dependency inside the company.

title: Power Follows the Cost of Switching
takeaway: A company gains bargaining power when its customer cannot replace it without costly delays, technical work, or approvals.
slide_title: Check: Size Does Not Set Leverage
body: The beginner's trap is to assume the largest company can always dictate terms. Correct that by asking whether it has a usable alternative before the next required delivery. A supplier can reject new commercial terms, subject to its existing obligations, while the buyer can reject nonconforming hardware; neither refusal creates replacement capacity. Dependence is also two-way: a supplier that needs one customer's orders cannot bargain without limits. At entry level, learn to record qualified sources and replacement lead times. As a senior buyer or supplier manager, use that evidence to negotiate and plan alternatives. At executive level, it informs whether to fund a second source, retain a supplier, or pursue ownership. The same reasoning supports a career in supply chain or supplier quality.

title: Power Follows the Cost of Switching
takeaway: A company gains bargaining power when its customer cannot replace it without costly delays, technical work, or approvals.
body: A company gains bargaining power when its customer cannot replace it without costly delays, technical work, or approvals. Before your interview, build a one-page replacement map for the Boeing–Spirit relationship using the acquisition announcement. Identify the buyer, the supplied product, the work another source would need, and who would accept its output. Mark any unknown cost or lead time as unknown rather than inventing it. Then explain the dependency aloud without notes, including why both parties have leverage. This develops a useful interview skill: turning a supplier relationship into a clear business judgment. Tomorrow, contract terms become necessary because companies must decide who carries the cost when a hard-to-replace supplier cannot deliver.

title: Power Comes From Costly Switching
takeaway: Bargaining power sits with the actor whose replacement would be hardest to qualify and put into service.
slide_title: The Logo Is Not The Map
body: An aircraft manufacturer's name is the most visible name on the product, but it is not the whole industry. Recall the map: the original equipment manufacturer integrates the aircraft; Tier 1 suppliers deliver directly to it; Tier 2 and Tier 3 suppliers work farther upstream; and maintenance, repair, and overhaul providers keep equipment operating. Those labels describe positions in a chain. Keep that map in view today as we move from identifying the participants to understanding their relationships.

title: Power Comes From Costly Switching
takeaway: Bargaining power sits with the actor whose replacement would be hardest to qualify and put into service.
body: Today's concept is leverage through qualified switching costs. It means that a seller gains bargaining power when its customer cannot easily move to an acceptable replacement. In aerospace, finding another machine shop is not the same as finding another usable part. The substitute must meet the required design and safety standards, have the necessary approval, and arrive in reliable quantities. Depending on the change, that can require engineering work, tests, documentation, and production preparation. A small supplier can therefore resist a large customer's demands when replacing it would cost the customer more than accepting its terms.

title: Power Comes From Costly Switching
takeaway: Bargaining power sits with the actor whose replacement would be hardest to qualify and put into service.
body: First, the aircraft manufacturer selects a system and pays a Tier 1 supplier under a purchase contract. That supplier buys components farther upstream. The approved aircraft design establishes which equipment and configurations are acceptable. Later, an operator pays a maintenance provider to keep the aircraft serviceable; that provider may buy a replacement component. If the component supplier raises its price, the buyer can ask for another source, but cannot simply install a similar-looking item. Someone must fund the engineering and approval work, establish reliable supply, and wait for the alternative. The regulator sets approval requirements, not commercial prices. Until a workable substitute exists, the incumbent supplier can refuse a price cut while the operator still needs a serviceable aircraft.

title: Power Comes From Costly Switching
takeaway: Bargaining power sits with the actor whose replacement would be hardest to qualify and put into service.
body: TransDigm shows why the company supplying a component can have more leverage than its place on the industry chart suggests. In its fiscal 2023 annual report, the aerospace component manufacturer estimated that approximately 90% of net sales came from proprietary products and approximately 80% came from products for which it was the sole-source provider. It reported $6.585 billion in net sales. The report also described aftermarket sales as historically about 55% of net sales. The outcome is a business that sells not only into new production, but also into an installed fleet needing replacement parts. Proprietary designs and sole-source positions make switching harder, though they do not make competition impossible. The wider lesson is that a purchase made during product design can shape a buyer's choices years later.

title: Power Comes From Costly Switching
takeaway: Bargaining power sits with the actor whose replacement would be hardest to qualify and put into service.
slide_title: Do Not Confuse Size With Power
body: The beginner's trap is to assume that the aircraft manufacturer always wins because it places the largest orders. Order volume matters, especially before a supplier wins a place on a new programme. After equipment enters service, however, the cost of replacing that supplier may change the balance. Nor does sole-source status mean permanent immunity from competition: the FAA's Parts Manufacturer Approval process provides a route for approved replacement and modification parts. The useful future question is therefore not merely whether demand will rise. Ask whether buyers are developing qualified alternatives. A second usable source can reduce the incumbent's leverage; another unapproved offer cannot do that yet.

title: Power Comes From Costly Switching
takeaway: Bargaining power sits with the actor whose replacement would be hardest to qualify and put into service.
body: Keep this sentence: Bargaining power sits with the actor whose replacement would be hardest to qualify and put into service. Test your understanding with a question: if an aircraft manufacturer and a component supplier both threaten to walk away, which one can obtain an acceptable replacement sooner, and who pays while they wait? Explain your answer through approval work, supply readiness, and the buyer's need to keep operating—not company size. Tomorrow's study of money earned after delivery follows naturally: once you know why a buyer stays, you can examine what that continuing relationship is worth.

title: Qualification Costs Shift Supplier Power
takeaway: Power sits with the supplier that is costly to replace, not necessarily with the company highest in the production chain.
slide_title: Recap: Position Is Not Investment Value
body: Yesterday's industry map separated the original equipment manufacturer, or OEM, from its suppliers and the maintenance, repair, and overhaul network, or MRO. Airbus delivers aircraft, Safran supplies major systems and equipment, and Lufthansa Technik maintains aircraft and components. Keep those roles clear when comparing businesses. A company's place in that chain tells you what it does, but it does not, by itself, establish the margins or cash flows that support its valuation. Today we stay with those same buyer and supplier relationships.

title: Qualification Costs Shift Supplier Power
takeaway: Power sits with the supplier that is costly to replace, not necessarily with the company highest in the production chain.
slide_title: Concept: The Cost Of Replacing Approval
body: Qualification-based switching costs are the money, testing, documentation, and time a buyer must spend to replace a component already accepted for a particular aircraft or system. The approved supplier gains leverage because a cheaper quote is not yet a usable substitute. Approval applies to a defined product and use; it is not a blanket monopoly. Investors should track the share of sales supplied without an approved rival, the availability of approved alternatives, and the time and cost of replacement. Then compare those claims with price increases, operating margins, and cash generation. Durable switching costs can support a higher valuation, but only if the supplier captures the benefit rather than spending it on quality failures or delivery penalties.

title: Qualification Costs Shift Supplier Power
takeaway: Power sits with the supplier that is costly to replace, not necessarily with the company highest in the production chain.
slide_title: Mechanism: A Quote Is Not Substitution
body: First, an OEM or major system supplier selects a component and demonstrates that the design meets its requirements. Second, replacing that component may require fresh engineering, testing, and approval evidence. The buyer funds or negotiates who funds that work; the design holder controls the design change, while the relevant approval authority can reject inadequate evidence. Third, an airline pays an MRO provider to restore an aircraft to service. The shop must use an eligible replacement, not merely the cheapest available part. The incumbent can therefore resist a price cut if substitution costs more than the saving. TransDigm illustrates the financial result investors investigate: fiscal 2024 sales were $7.940 billion, and its company-defined adjusted earnings measure, EBITDA As Defined, had a 52.6% margin. That is not an operating margin or proof that every product has equal power.

title: Qualification Costs Shift Supplier Power
takeaway: Power sits with the supplier that is costly to replace, not necessarily with the company highest in the production chain.
body: TransDigm reported that approximately 80% of fiscal 2024 net sales came from products for which it believed it was the sole-source provider. Sales increased from $6.585 billion in fiscal 2023 to $7.940 billion in fiscal 2024. Its EBITDA As Defined margin rose from 51.6% to 52.6%. The outcome was a component supplier earning substantial margins without being the aircraft manufacturer. Its positions within approved designs help explain why customers cannot always force prices down by requesting another quote. However, acquisitions and demand also affected results; these totals do not isolate the value of switching costs. Ask management: “For your largest sole-source products, what would a customer have to test, approve, and spend to replace you, and when could that replacement enter service?” A credible answer names the actual hurdles, not just a long customer relationship.

title: Qualification Costs Shift Supplier Power
takeaway: Power sits with the supplier that is costly to replace, not necessarily with the company highest in the production chain.
slide_title: Check: Sole Source Is Not Permanent
body: The beginner's trap is to treat “sole source” as “the customer has no choice forever.” It means the supplier currently occupies that position, not that an alternative cannot be approved. In civil aviation, the Federal Aviation Administration's Parts Manufacturer Approval process provides a route for eligible replacement parts. Buyers can also redesign systems or qualify another source when the expected savings justify the effort. Watch for new competing approvals, customer-funded replacement projects, and delivery or quality failures that make switching worth the trouble. Defense buyers may also hold technical data rights that make another source more practical. Supplier tiers describe distance from the OEM, not bargaining rank: even a small component maker can hold leverage, but only while the replacement burden remains meaningful.

title: Qualification Costs Shift Supplier Power
takeaway: Power sits with the supplier that is costly to replace, not necessarily with the company highest in the production chain.
body: Power sits with the supplier that is costly to replace, not necessarily with the company highest in the production chain. Put this into practice by choosing one supplier and reading its latest annual report for sole-source claims and competitive risks. For a major product, identify the buyer, the design decision-maker, any approved rival, and the work needed to switch. Mark undisclosed facts as unknown rather than assuming protection. Then compare the claimed advantage with margins and cash generation before paying a valuation premium. Tomorrow, examine contract terms, because the ability to resist replacement matters financially only when the agreement lets a company capture that advantage.

title: Qualified Suppliers Are Hard to Replace
takeaway: A qualified supplier gains leverage when replacing it forces the buyer to repeat costly approval work.
body: Yesterday, you worked on where a possible venture fits: the mission it serves, the customer it helps, and the work its product would replace. Keep that map in front of you. An airline carrying passengers, a defense customer buying capability, and a company supplying hardware occupy different positions, even when they touch the same vehicle. Today we will use those positions to ask a sharper question: who can say no when a possible venture proposes a change?

title: Qualified Suppliers Are Hard to Replace
takeaway: A qualified supplier gains leverage when replacing it forces the buyer to repeat costly approval work.
body: Qualification means demonstrating that a product meets the requirements for a particular use. Qualification creates switching costs when replacing that product requires new tests, engineering reviews, records, or approvals. An original equipment manufacturer, or OEM, integrates the finished vehicle. Tier 1 suppliers usually provide major systems; Tier 2 suppliers provide assemblies; Tier 3 suppliers provide parts or materials. These labels describe relationships, not a fixed ranking of power. The customer controlling acceptance can reject a proposed change, but an approved supplier can also have leverage if replacement would delay production or operation. Incumbents therefore buy a documented path to continued operation, not just a component. Your startup's opening is a problem worth paying to requalify, or a solution that reduces the work needed to make that change.

title: Qualified Suppliers Are Hard to Replace
takeaway: A qualified supplier gains leverage when replacing it forces the buyer to repeat costly approval work.
body: The chain starts when a buyer wants a new capability or a replacement supplier. The responsible engineering team sets requirements and identifies the evidence needed for acceptance. Someone then pays to build hardware, run tests, and close failures. Only after the required evidence is accepted can the new product enter its intended service. SpaceX illustrates a startup route through this barrier. In 2006, NASA selected it for an initial $278 million Commercial Orbital Transportation Services agreement. NASA paid against milestones; SpaceX supplied its own investment and development work. The commercial shift was toward an integrated station-cargo service, not merely a rocket launch. This was an expansion rather than an abandonment of its launch business. NASA controlled station access and acceptance; SpaceX controlled the vehicle design and its suppliers. The eventual outcome was a demonstrated cargo-delivery system. Money funded the evidence, and accepted evidence unlocked operation.

title: Qualified Suppliers Are Hard to Replace
takeaway: A qualified supplier gains leverage when replacing it forces the buyer to repeat costly approval work.
body: NASA's total COTS commitment to SpaceX eventually reached $396 million. Dragon was captured and berthed at the International Space Station on May 25, 2012, completing the central demonstration of access. Importantly, NASA had already awarded SpaceX a $1.6 billion contract for 12 cargo-resupply missions in December 2008. The first contracted resupply mission launched in October 2012. An award could therefore come before qualification was complete, but operational delivery still depended on clearing the gates. For a founder, the buyer was NASA's cargo program, while station integration and safety teams held acceptance authority. The sellable unit was a resupply service, not a cheap component. The route from the 2006 development agreement to operational service took years. Separate your development-funding proposal from your delivery price, and ask which approval milestones the customer's schedule can support.

title: Qualified Suppliers Are Hard to Replace
takeaway: A qualified supplier gains leverage when replacing it forces the buyer to repeat costly approval work.
slide_title: Check: Cheaper Does Not Mean Replaceable
body: The beginner's mistake is to compare the startup's price with the incumbent's price and call the difference customer savings. The real comparison also includes tests, engineering time, approval work, and the risk of interrupted service. body: Today's concept is customer-controlled supplier qualification: the process through which a buyer accepts a supplier's ability to make specified parts under agreed controls. Consider a startup selling flight-critical machined parts. The original equipment manufacturer, or OEM, builds the aircraft or engine. A Tier 1 supplier may deliver an assembly and buy your parts further down the chain. That direct customer applies its own requirements plus requirements passed down from the OEM. A quality-system certificate can help you enter the conversation, but it does not approve every part you could manufacture. This is where the structure resists change: available machine capacity is not automatically usable capacity. The opening for a newcomer is to deliver both the hardware and the evidence needed to accept it.

body: Start with the controlled drawing and purchase requirements. The buyer's engineering team defines what the part must satisfy; its quality team checks the supplier and required evidence; purchasing places the order once the required approvals are in place. Your startup plans machining, inspection, material traceability, and any special processes. It then makes the initial parts and records the results. Where AS9102 applies, first article inspection documents whether the production process produced a part meeting the specified requirements; it is not a blanket certificate for the factory. Your startup funds equipment and preparation unless the contract assigns those costs to the buyer. Parts and their records then move to the customer for acceptance. Hadrian's automated-factory model changes how this work is executed, not the customer's authority to accept it. The practical gap is a faster, more reliable path from drawing to acceptable evidence.

body: The beginner's trap is saying, “Once our factory has AS9100 certification, aerospace customers can buy any part from us.” The correction is that a quality-system certificate addresses how the business manages quality; customer acceptance also depends on the contracted part, process, records, and approval requirements. A capable machine and a correct sample do not remove those obligations. The real reason is risk: the buyer remains responsible for the parts it puts into its assembly. Before promising a delivery date, ask which approvals are required, who signs them, and what changes would trigger another review. A move to another site or a changed manufacturing process may require new evidence under the customer's rules. Build those rules into the pilot instead of discovering them after quoting.
